source.title: The Geometry of Refusal in Large Language Models: Concept Cones and Representational Independence
source.authors: Tom Wollschlager; Jannes Elstner; Simon Geisler; Vincent Cohen-Addad; Stephan Gunnemann; Johannes Gasteiger

record.tranche_reason: The study directly compares difference-in-means (DIM) refusal-direction interventions with other methods and reports that refusal is mediated by multi-dimensional cones and multiple independent directions, refining the single-direction claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports DIM directional-ablation results, DIM activation-addition results, benchmark scores under DIM ablation, and results on refusal cones and independent directions. Values used only to select or train directions are not recorded as results. RDO-specific results are not included unless they directly compare or test the claimed DIM-direction behavior. Cited results from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study reruns DIM directional ablation and activation addition on 7 chat models with ASR and capability benchmarks (V1). It then reports refusal-mediating cones and representationally independent directions whose combined ablation beats DIM, a direct argument for V4. The GCG experiment optimizes suffixes to suppress RepInd-1, not the DIM direction, so it does not test V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude refusal is better described by multi-dimensional polyhedral cones and multiple representationally independent directions than by one linear direction. They find orthogonality alone does not imply independence under intervention. They also conclude their gradient-based RDO finds refusal directions as effective as DIM with fewer side effects, notably on TruthfulQA.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces gradient-based Refusal Direction Optimization and cone optimization rather than relying only on the original DIM extraction. It does use DIM directions as explicit baselines and compares directional ablation and activation subtraction against them.
record.method_sensitivity: Cone performance varies with cone dimension and model size; for Gemma 2 2B, best-of-N ASR plateaus at four dimensions. The study also reports dependence on retain-loss weight and on the selected intervention direction.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating an RDO direction orthogonal to DIM reduces DIM's representation in later layers, and vice versa; orthogonality does not imply independence under intervention.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Geometrically orthogonal refusal directions are not causally independent under ablation.

fits_no_version.finding: GCG suffixes trained with a loss to suppress RepInd-1 reduce its representation and jailbreak 36% of the time, similar to RepInd-1 ablation ASR.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Non-DIM independent refusal directions are reachable from token-space inputs.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 267, 2025
record.problems: Many cone and representational-independence outcomes are presented only in figures without exact values in the text. RepInd-direction training has high variance across runs, and the authors note that all directions are optimized on the same targets, which may limit how distinct the mechanisms are.
record.rows_left_out: Table 5 also reports DIM activation-subtraction ASRs, which are not the directional-ablation operation named by V1 and are omitted. Table 1 and Table 4 provide additional or overlapping capability measurements; the Table 5 DIM-ablation benchmark values are retained instead. Further figure-only activation-addition, cone, and direction-sampling breakdowns are omitted to remain within the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: Only 7 chat models from three families (Gemma 2, Qwen 2.5, Llama 3); no larger or other families. Activation addition is figure-only.
No weight-edit or abliterated released models.
Whether ordinary jailbreaks suppress the DIM direction is not tested. Adversarial training against ablation is not tested. The GCG experiment targets RepInd-1 by design.

missing.what: DIM direction selection: for Qwen 2.5 7B only one (layer, token) DIM candidate both induces refusal and has low side effects; most Qwen 2.5 DIM directions have too-high side effects.
missing.locator: Section 4 'Is our method versatile?', Appendix D, Figure 16

missing.what: Ablating multiple DIM directions extracted from different layers does not improve ASR, unlike ablating multiple RepInd directions.
Cone directions induce refusal under addition at higher dimensions than under ablation; inducing refusal is easier than disabling it.
Gemma 2 2B cone lower bounds degrade significantly at dimension 5.
DIM activation-subtraction ASRs (e.g. Gemma 2 2B JBB 71.2), declared omitted but relevant to the 'adding/subtracting' half of V1.

record.verdict_notes: V3 was removed: the GCG attack is deliberately optimized to suppress RepInd-1 (not DIM), so it shows input accessibility, not that jailbreaks work via the refusal direction. ASR is judged with the StrongREJECT fine-tuned judge, which also scores response quality, so roughly 80% is near ceiling; both DIM and RDO plateau there. Most V4 evidence is figure-only, with no exact values in the text. The authors note RepInd directions share training targets and RepInd training has high run-to-run variance.

versions.untested_parts: Does not establish that one DIM direction completely removes every refusal or that every general capability is preserved; tests selected chat models and benchmark performance.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration experiment.
Tests a GCG suffix optimized to reduce RepInd-1 representation; does not test whether other jailbreaks generally suppress the DIM direction or whether training against ablation improves robustness.
Tests cones and independent directions in the evaluated chat models; does not establish that these geometries apply to all models.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment versus refusal decision.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or other transfer study.
Does not vary when or how refusal training was conducted.

relationships.condition: DIM ablation and addition in Gemma 2 2B/9B, Llama 3 8B, Qwen 2.5 3B/7B/14B
relationships.reason: DIM ablation lifts ASR from 0.3-22.7 to 63-82 on three benchmarks, matching the optimized RDO direction (R01-R03, R05-R10, R12-R17, R19-R21). MMLU, ARC-C and GSM8K stay within ~2.6 points (R22-R24, R26-R28, R30-R32, R34-R36, R38-R40, R42-R44, R46-R48). Addition induces refusal in all models (R50, figure only).

labels.reason: The text states cones up to dimension five in all tested models, RepInd directions significantly above a random vector, and top-k RepInd beating DIM for k>=4. Multi-cone sampling beats single RDO only at low N (Fig. 5).

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.condition: Higher cone dimension, smaller models, successive RepInd directions
labels.reason: Lower bounds degrade with dimension and degrade faster in smaller Qwen models (Fig. 4). Gemma 2 2B plateaus at 4, with degradation at 5 (Figs. 17, 19). ASR of successive RepInd directions declines (Fig. 7).

relation.reason: Its own DIM ablation and addition results, plus the cone and RepInd results, bear directly on V1 and V4.

tranche.reason: The study explicitly argues that the single-direction framing (Arditi et al.) needs restating, using multi-dimensional cones and representationally independent directions. It also reruns DIM ablation and addition on 7 chat models.

source_check.notes: Code is available (cs.cit.tum.de/daml/geometry-of-refusal), so the record's code: n is wrong. Rows and statements not in this pack's sample that rely on 'code n' need fixing. Not captured in rows: (1) ablating multiple DIM directions from different layers does not improve ASR (Sec. 6.1), relevant to V4; (2) Table 1 gives Qwen 2.5 14B DIM TruthfulQA as 63.3, while Table 5 gives 63.4. ASR is scored by the StrongREJECT fine-tuned judge, and all models top out near 80, so ASR is not a refusal rate.

statements.correction: Qwen 2.5 1.5B, DIM directional ablation (all layers and positions), StrongREJECT fine-tuned judge: JBB 0.4->53.1, StrongREJECT 3.1->65.2, SORRY-Bench 9.2->52.5. RDO on the same model: 53.5, 61.3, 49.1 (Table 5).
statements.problem: The numbers for this study are right. Caveat: ASR comes from the StrongREJECT fine-tuned judge, and every model tops out near 80. RDO is as low on Qwen 2.5 1.5B (53.5 / 61.3 / 49.1), so 53.1 ASR is not a direct measure of how much refusal is kept.

statements.correction: The paper states 'Resources & code: cs.cit.tum.de/daml/geometry-of-refusal'. Fig. 5 (Gemma 2 2B, 4-dim cone): sampling the cone beats temperature sampling at low N; at higher N, randomness dominates. Fig. 19: ASR rises with cone dimension and plateaus at four.
statements.problem: 'code n' is wrong: the paper gives code. Also, the best-of-N advantage over a temperature-sampled single RDO holds only in the low-sample regime (Fig. 5).

statements.correction: The high variance in RepInd training is stated in Appendix A.3: five candidates per direction, lowest validation refusal score kept.
The text also says larger Qwen models appear to support higher-dimensional cones (Section 5). Gemma 2 2B lower bounds degrade significantly at dimension 5 (Fig. 17).
Source: Appendix E, Figure 18, Qwen 2.5 family. Most directions, even in high-dimensional cones, still induce refusal under addition.

Table 5, TruthfulQA under DIM ablation: drops of 3.0-8.3 points across all 7 models (Qwen 2.5 3B 57.2->54.2; Gemma 2 9B 61.1->52.8). The 3.6-8.3 range comes from Table 4, which omits Qwen 2.5 3B. Code: cs.cit.tum.de/daml/geometry-of-refusal.
statements.problem: The TruthfulQA drop range is wrong at the low end: Qwen 2.5 3B drops 3.0, not at least 3.6. 'code n' is wrong.
